L198: Agent Diff addresses these limitations simultaneously. Our containerized replicas of production APIs provide ecological fidelity with full reproducibility – without the temporal instability of live services or the oversimplification of mocked environments. Deterministic state diffing evaluates what changed rather than how, capturing both intended outcomes and unintended side effects – unlike goal-state comparison, response diffing, or trace matching.
L199: And by targeting code-executing agents against black-box enterprise APIs, we fill the gap left by code-execution benchmarks that assume white-box access.
L200: ## 3. Agent-Diff
L201: 
L202: Agent-Diff evaluates code-execution agents on long-horizon enter- prise API tasks and evaluates how state changed in the environment. The framework requires: (i) black-box equivalence – closed-source APIs can be faithfully replicated from their public contracts; (ii) state-centric modeling – all operations reduce to typed, state transitions that can be diffed; and (iii) deterministic isolation – each run starts from an identical snapshot.
L203: ### 3.1. Agent-Diff Environments
L204: 
L205: Our central design hypothesis is that closed-source enterprise APIs can be replicated with sufficient fidelity to produce representative evaluation scores because the contract – not the implementation – defines correctness from an agent’s perspective.
L206: Consider an API as a function $f:(\mathcal{R},S)\rightarrow(S^{\prime},\mathcal{O})$ mapping requests and state to new state and outputs. An agent observes only $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{O}$; the internal path from $S$ to $S^{\prime}$ is opaque.
L207: 
L208: Two implementations $f$ and $\hat{f}$ are behaviorally equivalent over $\mathcal{R}^{*}$ if:
L209: 
L210: (1)  |  | $$\forall\,r\in\mathcal{R}^{*},\,S:\;f(r,S)=\hat{f}(r,S)$$  |
L211: Full equivalence over all possible requests is neither achievable nor necessary. We target equivalence over the subset $\mathcal{R}^{*}\subset\mathcal{R}$ exercised by the benchmark tasks. Because the APIs in our benchmark are predominantly CRUD interfaces over typed entities, internal side effects (notifications, analytics, caching) are invisible to the agent and irrelevant for evaluation – our replicas need only produce equivalent outputs for equivalent inputs.
L212: Crucially, all information required to construct $\hat{f}$ is publicly available: entity schemas (via OpenAPI or GraphQL introspection), operation semantics, response formats (via official SDKs), and error conditions (【159†Slack Technologies, 2026b】; 【160†Box, Inc., 2026a】; 【161†Google LLC, 2026】; 【162†Linear Inc., 2026b】). We validate replica fidelity through automated conformance testing against production APIs and adversarial edge-case probing (Appendix 【105†8.10】).
L213: ##### State-Centric Modelling.
L214: 
L215: We model each service as a state machine where state $S$ is a typed relational database. Entity types (User, Channel, Message in Slack; File, Folder in Box, etc.) map to tables with schemas derived from public API specifications. All operations reduce to three transitions:
L216: (2)  |  | Insert  | $\displaystyle:S\rightarrow S\cup\{e\}$  |
L217: (3)  |  | Update  | $\displaystyle:S\rightarrow(S\setminus\{e\})\cup\{e^{\prime}\}$  |
L218: (4)  |  | Delete  | $\displaystyle:S\rightarrow S\setminus\{e\}$  |
L219: 
L220: Rather than validating API call traces, we snapshot all tables before and after agent execution and compute the state difference:
L221: (5)  |  | $\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{add}}$  | $\displaystyle=T_{\text{after}}\setminus T_{\text{before}}$  |
L222: (6)  |  | $\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{del}}$  | $\displaystyle=T_{\text{before}}\setminus T_{\text{after}}$  |
L223: (7)  |  | $\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{mod}}$  | $\displaystyle=\{(e,e^{\prime}):e.\text{pk}=e^{\prime}.\text{pk}\land e\neq e^{\prime}\}$  |
L224: 
L225: The resulting DiffResult – containing all inserted, deleted, and modified entities – is compared against the task’s expected state changes.
L226: ##### Deterministic Isolation.
L227: 
L228: Each benchmark run instantiates a fresh, isolated environment. We leverage PostgreSQL’s schema isolation: each environment operates within its own schema namespace (e.g., state_{env_id}), enabling concurrent execution without cross-contamination. Environments are seeded from deterministic templates, ensuring identical initial states $S_{0}$ across runs. This architecture guarantees that for any task $\tau$ and agent $\mathcal{A}$:
L229: (8)  |  | $$\forall r_{1},r_{2}\in\text{Runs}(\tau,\mathcal{A}):S_{0}^{(r_{1})}=S_{0}^{(r_{2})}$$  |
L230: enabling reproducible evaluation without the temporal instability of live APIs. To support state diffing, we snapshot all entity tables immediately before and after agent execution, creating immutable copies $T_{\text{before}}$ and $T_{\text{after}}$ within the same isolated schema. Because each environment is fully independent, snapshots are free from interference by concurrent runs, and the resulting diffs reflect only the actions of the evaluated agent.

L315: Figure 【166†2】 shows the assertions for a two-step Box task (“Delete the misfiled copy, then tag the correct one”). The first assertion checks that the misfiled file was removed (deleted); the second verifies that the tag was applied (updated). Because this task has $|A(\tau)|=2$ assertions, it contributes weight 2 to the aggregate score – a task with 10 assertions would contribute weight 10, ensuring that complex multi-step tasks are not underrepresented.

L317: Figure 2. Example assertion set for a two-step task. diff_type specifies which partition of the state diff to query: added = entities present in $S_{1}$ but not $S_{0}$; deleted = entities in $S_{0}$ but not $S_{1}$; updated = entities whose primary key persists but one or more field values changed. The where clause filters by field-level predicates; expected_count sets the required number of matching rows. This task contributes $m(\tau)=2$ to the denominator of the aggregate score.
L318: ##### Closed-world invariant.
L319: Let $A(\tau)$ denote the set of required assertions for task $\tau$ and $F(\tau)$ the set of fields explicitly marked as ignored. Each task’s assertion set and ignore-list has been manually reviewed to exclude non-deterministic third-order effects (e.g., updated_at timestamps) while capturing all semantically meaningful state changes. We enforce a closed-world invariant: every entity change in $\Delta S(\tau)$ must be accounted for by some assertion in $A(\tau)$ or involve only fields in $F(\tau)$.
L320: Any unaccounted diff – an unexpected insertion, deletion, or field mutation – is treated as a side effect and the task score is set to zero. Formally,
L321: (11)  |  | $$\mathrm{clean}(\tau)=\mathbb{1}\big[\Delta S(\tau)\setminus\mathrm{cover}(A(\tau),F(\tau))=\emptyset\big],$$  |
L322: 
L323: where $\mathrm{cover}$ denotes the set of diffs explained by assertions or ignored fields. This prevents an agent from achieving a high score by completing the requested actions while simultaneously corrupting unrelated state.
L324: ##### Scoring metrics.
L325: 
L326: Let $\mathrm{sat}(a,\Delta S)\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether assertion $a$ holds on the state diff. We define three metrics:
L327: 
L328: Pass rate. A binary indicator of full task completion with no side effects:
L329: 
L330: (12)  |  | $$\mathrm{Pass}(\tau)=\mathrm{clean}(\tau)\cdot\mathbb{1}\Big[\bigwedge_{a\in A(\tau)}\mathrm{sat}(a,\Delta S)=1\Big].$$  |
L331: Score. An assertion-weighted measure that gives proportionally more credit to complex tasks. Each task contributes $s(\tau)=\mathrm{clean}(\tau)\cdot\sum_{a\in A(\tau)}\mathrm{sat}(a,\Delta S)$ out of a maximum $m(\tau)=|A(\tau)|$. The aggregate score across a task set $\mathcal{T}$ is
L332: 
L333: (13)  |  | $$\mathrm{Score}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}s(\tau)}{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}m(\tau)},$$  |
L334: so a 10-assertion task that passes 8 assertions but triggers an unexpected deletion contributes $(0,10)$, not $(8,10)$. This weighting ensures that long-horizon tasks with many verification points are not underrepresented relative to simple single-assertion tasks.
L335: ## 5. Experiments
L336: 
L337: ### 5.1. Experiment Setup
L338: 
L339: ##### Prompting & Interaction.
L340: 
L341: We utilize the ReAct prompting framework (【167†Yao et al., 2023b】) adapted for code execution. The system prompt 【90†8.6】 instructs the model to reason about the task and emit a code block (Bash) to interact with the environment.
L465: We introduced Agent-Diff, a benchmark for code-executing LLM agents on enterprise API tasks. Containerized replicas of production APIs provide ecological fidelity with full reproducibility, and a state-diff evaluation contract enables reproducible, declarative assertions that verify expected state changes while enforcing a closed-world invariant to detect unintended side effects.
L466: Evaluating nine models across 224 tasks, we find scores ranging from 38.0 to 88.1, with documentation effects that are service- and model-specific: pass rates improve significantly ($+7.0$ pp, $P=1.00$) while assertion-weighted scores do not ($+2.4$, $P=0.73$). A training-cutoff natural experiment validates our inclusion of recently introduced endpoints, which isolate inference-time learning from pre-training memorization.

L597: ## The next controls to build.
L598: 
L599: The repository documents where the boundary sits today and what each next step is. These are the four largest.
L600: 
L601: ### Demonstrate cancelling a live turn
L602: 
L603: An operator can already cancel a turn mid-flight, and the code path discards it under a named rule. Recording that moment is next: no turn in the committed evidence pack was cancelled yet.
L604: ### Look inside encrypted tunnels
L605: 
L606: Today an allowed HTTPS destination is matched by exact host and port, and the hold control covers plain HTTP. Inspecting inside the tunnel is the next control to build.

L609: 
L610: 902 of 5,005 ordinary turns were sent to a person rather than stopped. The corpus report names the two rules that carry almost all of it, and each can be tuned with a one-line change.
L611: ### Grow from one host to a fleet
L612: 
L613: The store is a single-process JSON store, and ordinary containers are not a hardened multi-tenant boundary. The replacement points for both are documented in the repository.

L57: An AI coding agent is given a task and a shell. When it finishes, it tells you what it did. That report is not always true.
L58: In a recorded run against a real model, the agent closed its turn with a confident summary: all steps complete, the CLI created, both tests passing. The journal for the same turn recorded nine commands and six failures, including the test command itself exiting with an error. Nobody scripted this. It is an ordinary run, captured while it happened, and the capture is committed in the repository.
L59: Most agent platforms decide what is safe before a turn runs, by reading the text of a command. Commands can be spelled in ways a classifier has not seen, and destinations can be built at runtime. Shadow Commit decides after the turn runs, from what actually changed. Effects do not need to be guessed. They can be counted.
L60: 
L61: The policy reads the recorded changes rather than the agent's summary.

L79: 03 The idea
L80: ## Each turn passes through five stages and ends in one decision.
L81: 
L82: Shadow Commit wraps the platform's own agent runner in a transaction. The agent is never told it is wrapped. The five stages below run on every turn of every agent.
L83: 
L84: The turn seal
L85: 
L86: 1 Seal seal.fallback
L87: 
L88: 2 Run turn.begin · turn.executed
L89: 
L90: 3 Capture effects.captured
L91: 
L92: 4 Judge policy.decision
L93: 
L94: 5 Settle turn.committed / discarded / held
L95: 
L96: Stage 1 Seal
L97: ### The workspace is copied before anything runs.
L98: 
L99: Before the turn starts, the platform copies the workspace and records every file. The agent's memory, the notes it keeps between turns, is sealed the same way. A private network comes up for this one turn, and its only route out is the broker, a proxy the platform controls that forwards only approved outbound requests.
L100: 
L101: The real workspace is not reachable from inside the turn.
L102: 
L103: Stage 2 Run
L104: ### The agent works normally, on the copy.
L105: 
L106: The real Codex CLI runs inside a container against the sealed copy. It receives a workspace path exactly as it always did. It writes files, runs commands, and continues its session. Nothing about the agent changes.
L107: 
L108: The runner is the starter kit's own agent runner, wrapped once so the agent cannot tell.
L109: 
L110: Stage 3 Capture
L111: ### Everything that changed becomes one list.
L112: 
L113: When the turn ends, the platform computes the difference between the sealed copy and what the agent left behind: every file created, modified, or deleted, plus every outbound network write the broker held back. That list is called the effect set. Every changed file is hashed.
L114: 
L115: The effect set is the complete record of the turn, independent of what the agent says.
L116: 
L117: Stage 4 Judge
L118: ### Eighteen rules read the effect set as a whole.
L119:
